A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SongGen. All 13 pages of v1 and 14 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support reliable comparison. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D report original song-generation evaluations, listener ratings, ablations and codec experiments.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix C retain original experiments and add multi-stage baseline results, additional automatic metrics and generation timings.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2-3.5 retain the same tokenization, mixed and dual-track procedures, auxiliary vocal loss, conditioning modules, preprocessing and training scheme. The new multi-stage system is a comparison baseline, not a modification of SongGen.

E1.justification: Both versions use approximately 540K English song clips from MSD, FMA and MTG-Jamendo and evaluate on the same 326 MusicCaps samples. Generation with and without reference voices is retained. Rap and ballad examples added to the motivation do not establish additional evaluated scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 replaces Stable Audio Open and MusicGen in the main comparisons with a newly evaluated two-stage vocal-then-accompaniment baseline using SongGen's component architecture and training data. Parler-TTS and the human comparison with Suno remain. This substantially changes the relevance and composition of the comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 adds CLaMP3, four aesthetics metrics and a timed 30-second generation comparison. Its new multi-stage experiment uses two separately trained 200K-step models and omits voice-free support. These additions substantially expand evaluation, while the existing dataset selection, normalization, reference inputs and listener sample sizes remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds qualitative codec failure analysis, reporting lyric-following failures, noise and silence for Encodec and DAC without quantifying their rates. The existing training-strategy, lyric-integration and codec ablations, attention visualizations and loss curves are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Tables 2-3 add ± values to human ratings that v1 reported only as means. Five generation seeds and 36 samples evaluated by 20 listeners were already documented. v2 does not define the ± statistic or establish that additional runs were performed.

E6.justification: Retained scores are unchanged, but v2 adds multi-stage results, ground-truth automatic scores, CLaMP3/aesthetics results and latency measurements, while removing Stable Audio Open/MusicGen results. Newly reported comparisons show Mixed Pro versus multi-stage overall quality of 3.96 versus 3.39, PER of 40.58 versus 38.80, and generation times of 18.04 versus 42.85 seconds. These are new comparisons, not improvements over v1's SongGen scores.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and Equations 1-4 are unchanged. The new discussion of joint versus separately optimized vocal/accompaniment distributions is conceptual interpretation, without a new formal result, assumption or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add explicit claims that multi-stage error accumulation harms quality and that SongGen outperforms the multi-stage baseline. The central contributions—single-stage controllable generation, two output modes and the data pipeline—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving cross-stage errors and vocal/accompaniment coordination, and attributes the baseline's PER/SECS advantage to clean-vocal training. Appendix C tempers v1's strong semantic-feature explanation for X-Codec by acknowledging possible pretraining-data effects and reconstruction-quality tradeoffs. Appendix B also questions CLAP reliability. The existing duration and sampling-rate limitations are merely relocated.

D1.justification: v2 documents the multi-stage baseline's implementation and training, A800 timing hardware, metric software packages, and the exact X-Codec checkpoint with its 200K-hour pretraining provenance. Code and training configurations change from promised to reported available. Existing SongGen implementation settings remain unchanged; these disclosures do not establish a changed codec or training corpus.

R1.justification: Related work adds MusicGen-Stem and YuE, contrasting YuE's scaling and two-stage design with SongGen's token-pattern approach. References also add CLaMP3, Audiobox Aesthetics and AudioSet. These update the research context without replacing the overall positioning.

P1.justification: The motivation, baseline discussion and codec appendix receive localized rewrites and expansions. The limitations paragraph moves unchanged from Appendix A to main-text Section 5; acknowledgments and affiliation/publication details are added. The method exposition and conclusion remain essentially unchanged.

P2.justification: The combined v1 Table 1 becomes separate automatic and human evaluation tables, with grouped metric headings and uncertainty notation. Later tables are renumbered and figures repositioned; Figure 1's caption changes. All six figure graphics are retained, making this a targeted presentation revision.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked a controlled song-generation comparator for its central single-stage argument. v2's multi-stage baseline and quality/latency comparisons substantially address that deficiency while acknowledging the baseline's PER/SECS advantage. Metric implementation details and more cautious codec attribution also improve transparency. Instrumental comparator coverage is reduced, MOS uncertainties remain undefined, and the baseline's Step-1-based training limits causal conclusions, but the new task-relevant evidence provides a substantial net improvement.
